cues.text: TriedPath Fellowship presents:
Understanding Your Roots.
Part one. How your mind works.
Our mind works like a computer.

It is constantly placing
information into categories.

If you feed something
destructive into your mind,

it will add this to a stack of
similar material already there.

As the stack grows larger, it
gains in power.

In the computer industry, the
saying is:
garbage in, garbage out.

It is our responsibility to see
that the new information

we receive is consistent with
our new life.

>> New from TriedPath: Mountains
of Material!

Scripture memory, on twelve
cassettes.

In the car. In the kitchen. At
your bedside.
Fill your memory tapes,
and push the old material out!
Operators are standing by!
End of part one. Question two.

Have you ever been able to stop
thinking about something?
Did you succeed?

Pause the tape, and write your
answer.
Part two. Your roots.
You were not born this way.
It grew, one response at a time.

And what was learned can be
unlearned.

A child's security rests on
three bonds:

mother to child, father to
child,
and father to mother.

Any break in this triangle
produces insecurity.
Real, or only perceived,
the results are the same.
>> The TriedPath Pocket Library.
Thirteen little booklets.

The roots, the way out, and help
for the family.
Just one dollar each.

Between two and six, a boy must
leave his mother's world,

and his father must welcome him
into his own.

But a boy with no welcome from
his father
finds none among the boys.

So he stays in the kitchen, with
his mother.

>> Roots and Recovery. Now on
video.
The developmental factors,
and nine proven principles.
Twenty dollars.

He compares himself with other
boys.
Comparison becomes admiration.
Admiration slips into envy.

At puberty, the envy becomes
eroticized.

>> Un-Walk Steps. A weekly class
for men.
Lessons read. Homework done.
Pen and binder in hand.
Keep a journal. And be on time.
Part three. Displacement.
Putting off, putting on.

Displacement is the idea that
one thing pushes out another.
There is no neutral ground.

If there is a vacancy there,
evil will fill it.

Interference is the technical
name for displacement.

New material coming into your
mind
pushes the old material out.

In thirty days, we forget eighty
percent
of what we learned.
For you, that is a blessing.

Turn on any radio or television,
and you will find

a mind-boggling barrage of new
morality propaganda.

Gays on television are shown as
superior people.
What do we lose?

The associations, triggered by
music, clothing,
and many other things.

Bars will close. The scene will
change.
Question five.

What do you do when associations
from the past overwhelm you?

Pause the tape, and write your
answer.

So fill your memory tapes with
new material,

until the bulk of it ejects the
old.

We forget things that are
contrary to our opinions.

If we are ambivalent, the new
information

will find no permanent home in
our minds.

This places the burden directly
on us.
>> You may be saying:

"I don't want to go to this
class!"
Women Relating to Men.

For all married and single
women.
Thursday, at seven-thirty.

Don't end up saying: "I wish I
had gone."
For further study:

booklet one, from our Pocket
Library.

Homosexual people say they never
asked
for their orientation.
In most cases, that is true.
Something they never chose.

breakLong.title: What this teaching asked of people
breakLong.intro: TriedPath Fellowship is invented. Its teaching is not: every lesson on this tape comes from a ministry handbook, booklets and a class manual used between 1993 and 1996, and every commercial from a real product, price or flyer of the time. These papers are kept in the Smithsonian's Love in Action Collection. This is what the teaching asked of the people it was written for, in its own words where it can be quoted.

sections.heading: What it asked of the person

items.text: To guard every thought that went in. “It is our responsibility to see that the new information we receive is consistent with our new life.” The handbook's rule for the mind was the computer saying “garbage in/garbage out”.
items.source: Love in Action, Helping People Step Out of Homosexuality (“a handbook for pastors, counselors, lay workers”), revised edition © 1995 (first published © 1984 as Steps Out of Homosexuality), Smithsonian National Museum of American History, Archives Center, NMAH.AC.1428 (the Mattachine Society of Washington “Love in Action” Collection), Box 2 Folder 13, printed p. 130 (PDF p. 138) and p. 131 (PDF p. 139); read on the page image, 15 Nov 2026

items.text: To turn off the radio and the television: “Turn on any radio or television and you will find a mind-boggling barrage of new morality propaganda. … Gays on television are shown as superior people.”
items.source: Love in Action, Helping People Step Out of Homosexuality (“a handbook for pastors, counselors, lay workers”), revised edition © 1995 (first published © 1984 as Steps Out of Homosexuality), Smithsonian National Museum of American History, Archives Center, NMAH.AC.1428 (the Mattachine Society of Washington “Love in Action” Collection), Box 2 Folder 13, printed pp. 130–131 (PDF pp. 138–139); read on the page image, 15 Nov 2026

items.text: To give up their music, their clothes, their bars and their scene. Under “What Do We Lose?” the handbook listed “the associations, triggered by music, clothing and many other things”, and promised that “bars will close, the scene will change”. It called “returning to old haunts” and “reviving the old associations that music brings forth” the way “an ex-gay person stumbles”.
items.source: Love in Action, Helping People Step Out of Homosexuality (“a handbook for pastors, counselors, lay workers”), revised edition © 1995 (first published © 1984 as Steps Out of Homosexuality), Smithsonian National Museum of American History, Archives Center, NMAH.AC.1428 (the Mattachine Society of Washington “Love in Action” Collection), Box 2 Folder 13, printed p. 132 (PDF p. 140) and p. 135 (PDF p. 143); read on the page image, 15 Nov 2026

items.text: To cut off their friends: “Yes, we are the ones who must cut off relationships with those that would keep us in bondage to sin.”
items.source: Love in Action, Helping People Step Out of Homosexuality (“a handbook for pastors, counselors, lay workers”), revised edition © 1995 (first published © 1984 as Steps Out of Homosexuality), Smithsonian National Museum of American History, Archives Center, NMAH.AC.1428 (the Mattachine Society of Washington “Love in Action” Collection), Box 2 Folder 13, printed p. 133 (PDF p. 141); read on the page image, 15 Nov 2026

items.text: To fill the mind until the old life was pushed out: Bible study, prayer and Scripture memorization, “adding mountains of material to your memory tapes. It will be this bulk of the material that ejects the desires and temptations of the old way of life.”
items.source: Love in Action, Helping People Step Out of Homosexuality (“a handbook for pastors, counselors, lay workers”), revised edition © 1995 (first published © 1984 as Steps Out of Homosexuality), Smithsonian National Museum of American History, Archives Center, NMAH.AC.1428 (the Mattachine Society of Washington “Love in Action” Collection), Box 2 Folder 13, printed p. 130 (PDF p. 138) and p. 132 (PDF p. 140); read on the page image, 15 Nov 2026

items.text: To come to every class on time, “lessons read, homework done, pen and binder in hand”, to keep a journal, to take notes at each session, and to spend time each week reflecting on the last session and share it at the next meeting.
items.source: Love in Action, Steps Out Program Class Manual (c. 1994; its latest dated item is June 1994), Smithsonian National Museum of American History, Archives Center, NMAH.AC.1428 (the Mattachine Society of Washington “Love in Action” Collection), Box 13 Folder 1, Program Overview p. iii (PDF p. 6): “KEEP A JOURNAL!”, “TAKE NOTES at each session”, “Spend time each week reflecting on last week's session. Share at the next meeting”; Group Interaction p. v (PDF p. 16): “Be on time!”, “Come prepared—lessons read, homework done, pen and binder in hand.”; read on the page image, 15 Nov 2026

items.text: To treat the group as their new family: “Our families were imperfect at best and corrupt at worst. God has given us the opportunity for a new family.” The same page counted on peer pressure: “Peer pressure (group reinforcement) … can play an equally important part in bringing a person out of the gay lifestyle.”
items.source: Love in Action, Steps Out Program Class Manual (c. 1994; its latest dated item is June 1994), Smithsonian National Museum of American History, Archives Center, NMAH.AC.1428 (the Mattachine Society of Washington “Love in Action” Collection), Box 13 Folder 1, Group Interaction p. i (PDF p. 12); read on the page image, 15 Nov 2026

items.text: If they could, to move away for a year. The handbook called a residential programme “by far, the most effective way”, said that relocating “in itself is often helpful in breaking sinful relationships and patterns”, and asked those who joined to “set aside other life goals” and commit to “a one-year period”, with a “$20.00 non-refundable fee” to receive an application.

items.text: To accept that this would be “the most difficult task of your entire life”.

sections.heading: Where it told them to look for the cause

items.text: In their families: “We believe that the deepest root of homosexuality is a break in the relational bonds within the family.” Any break in the bond of mother, father and child “will produce insecurity in the child … whether the break is real or only perceived by the child, the results are the same.”
items.source: Love in Action, Helping People Step Out of Homosexuality (“a handbook for pastors, counselors, lay workers”), revised edition © 1995 (first published © 1984 as Steps Out of Homosexuality), Smithsonian National Museum of American History, Archives Center, NMAH.AC.1428 (the Mattachine Society of Washington “Love in Action” Collection), Box 2 Folder 13, printed p. 13 (PDF p. 21); read on the page image, 15 Nov 2026

cues.text: [upbeat music]
Is a friendship getting too close?
The little booklet with the checklist.
Order a five-pack for your group.

Grab your journal and
your workbook, friend.
Today we go underneath.
Every tree is known by its fruit.

But fruit grows from roots,
and roots grow in soil.

For women, the classic teaching
names three things in the soil:

our relationships, our identity,
and how we picture God.
It's not a sexual orientation problem.
It's an identity crisis.
Let's pause the DVD here, friend.

Turn to page thirty-one, and
talk it through with your group.

A little girl first learns
who she is from her mother.

If Mom seems distant,
critical or overbearing,
she may pull back to protect herself.

The teaching calls it
defensive detachment.
A girl looks to her mother for the model,
and to her father for the grade.
His words become her score card:
passing or failing as a little girl.
[upbeat music]
Twenty Monday evenings.

A hundred and fifty dollars
covers your materials.
Ask about payment plans.
Groups fill up in days!

Here's a picture from an
older teaching — 1993.
Remember floppy disks?

To use a computer analogy,
a heterosexual woman
has a floppy disc that is titled “woman,”

so each experience that is
related to her femaleness
can be stored in that file.

The lesbian woman receives
information relating to femininity,
but she has no file to put it in.
The “information” and experiences
that should affirm her get lost.
Save that one, friend.

Emotional dependency is
when someone else's presence
feels necessary for your security.

When anyone takes the
centre that belongs to God,
the old booklet calls it idolatry.
Here are the signs.
Whether or not anything physical happens,
sin has entered the friendship.

Now, many of these things
aren't sinful in themselves.

Romantic gestures and
certain kinds of exclusivity

are completely appropriate
in marriage and engagement.

…and sometimes even in a
serious dating relationship.
[music stops]

breakLong.title: What this teaching asked of women
breakLong.intro: Heartwood is an invented DVD course. Its teaching is not: every lesson in it comes from booklets and courses sold to women and women's groups between 1987 and 2016. This is what that teaching asked of the women it was sold to, in its own words where it can be quoted.

sections.heading: What it asked of a woman

items.text: To end her closest friendship. When a friendship with another woman became “dependent”, the booklet said “a parting of the ways must take place”, and, where it had been “a lifelong pattern”, that “ties need to be broken with all past partners as well”.
items.source: Emotional Dependency: A Threat to Close Friendships (InterVarsity Press, 1990; first published by Love in Action, 1984, and by Exodus International–North America, 1987), Smithsonian NMAH.AC.1428 Box 2 Folder 9, printed p. 24 (PDF p. 30) and p. 20 (PDF p. 28), read on the page images

items.text: To throw away the songs they had shared: the booklet praised getting rid of “certain record albums or tapes (the ones containing ‘our song’)”.
items.source: Emotional Dependency: A Threat to Close Friendships (InterVarsity Press, 1990; first published by Love in Action, 1984, and by Exodus International–North America, 1987), Smithsonian NMAH.AC.1428 Box 2 Folder 9, printed p. 25 (PDF p. 30), read on the page image

items.text: To expect the loss to hurt like a marriage ending, and to call it healing: “Prepare for grief and depression. Letting go of a dependent relationship can be as painful as going through a divorce.”
items.source: Emotional Dependency: A Threat to Close Friendships (InterVarsity Press, 1990; first published by Love in Action, 1984, and by Exodus International–North America, 1987), Smithsonian NMAH.AC.1428 Box 2 Folder 9, printed p. 25 (PDF p. 30), read on the page image

items.text: To confess her feelings to another Christian, and to give that person “the freedom to periodically ask how things are going”.
items.source: Emotional Dependency: A Threat to Close Friendships (InterVarsity Press, 1990; first published by Love in Action, 1984, and by Exodus International–North America, 1987), Smithsonian NMAH.AC.1428 Box 2 Folder 9, printed pp. 22–23 (PDF p. 29), read on the page image

items.text: To watch her friendships for “warning signs”: wanting time alone together, being jealous when the friend sees others, making no plans without her, pet names and private jokes, wearing each other's clothes, poetry or “our song”, moving in together.
items.source: Emotional Dependency: A Threat to Close Friendships (InterVarsity Press, 1990; first published by Love in Action, 1984, and by Exodus International–North America, 1987), Smithsonian NMAH.AC.1428 Box 2 Folder 9, printed pp. 8–9 and 15 (PDF pp. 22–25)

items.text: To read the same gestures as sin between two women and as right between a man and a woman: “Romantic gestures and certain kinds of exclusivity are completely appropriate in marriage and engagement … and sometimes even in a serious dating relationship.”
items.source: Emotional Dependency: A Threat to Close Friendships (InterVarsity Press, 1990; first published by Love in Action, 1984, and by Exodus International–North America, 1987), Smithsonian NMAH.AC.1428 Box 2 Folder 9, printed pp. 16–17 (PDF p. 26)

sections.heading: Where it told her to look for the cause

items.text: In her mother: a mother “perceived as distant, bitter, critical, overbearing and unloving”, from whom a little girl was said to pull back in “defensive detachment”.
items.source: Focus on the Family, The Heart of the Matter: The Roots and Causes of Female Homosexuality (© 2001), Smithsonian NMAH.AC.1428 Box 6 Folder 4, printed p. 17 (PDF p. 11)

items.text: In her father: “The responses from her father produce the score card of passing or failing as a little girl.”
items.source: Exodus International–North America, Are People Born Gay? (booklet #PR-02, © 1993), Smithsonian NMAH.AC.1428 Box 2 Folder 12, printed p. 8 (PDF p. 6)

items.text: In her family as a whole: her attractions, it said, developed “because of the breakdown in a girl's initial relationship with her family—mother and father”.
items.source: Focus on the Family, The Heart of the Matter: The Roots and Causes of Female Homosexuality (© 2001), Smithsonian NMAH.AC.1428 Box 6 Folder 4, printed p. 14 (PDF p. 10)

items.text: In who she was: “The lesbian struggle is not a sexual orientation problem; it is an identity crisis.”
items.source: Focus on the Family, The Heart of the Matter: The Roots and Causes of Female Homosexuality (© 2001), Smithsonian NMAH.AC.1428 Box 6 Folder 4, printed p. 14 (PDF p. 10)

items.text: In a missing file: “The lesbian woman receives information relating to femininity, but she has no file to put it in.” A 1993 computer analogy; the tape reads it word for word.
items.source: Exodus International–North America, Are People Born Gay? (booklet #PR-02, © 1993), Smithsonian NMAH.AC.1428 Box 2 Folder 12, printed p. 19 (PDF p. 11), read on the page image

items.text: It blamed her. Counsellors, the booklet said, might realise after every kind of help that “this individual has no true interest in changing”.
items.source: Emotional Dependency: A Threat to Close Friendships (InterVarsity Press, 1990; first published by Love in Action, 1984, and by Exodus International–North America, 1987), Smithsonian NMAH.AC.1428 Box 2 Folder 9, printed p. 20 (PDF p. 28), read on the page image

Free.

breakLong.intro: HEDGE™ is an invented course for parents. Its reasons are not: each one was taught by a real ministry, newsletter, book, web page or campaign between 1988 and 2026, and some of them were first taught about gay people. This is what that teaching said and asked, in its own words where it can be quoted, with what is known beside it.

sections.heading: It said nobody knew the cause, then listed causes
